claims.text: Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 has a terminal tensile strain of approximately 13.5%.
Baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 exhibits excellent or demonstrated impact-triggered energy release.
HfZrTiTa0.53 currently has limited tensile ductility.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at.% Nb will promote Nb segregation to grain boundaries in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at.% Nb will produce finely dispersed, ductile second-phase precipitates in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Nb segregation will reduce intergranular stress concentrations.
Nb segregation will facilitate grain-boundary sliding.
The proposed ductile second phase will intercept crack propagation.
The proposed grain-boundary and second-phase changes will improve uniform tensile deformation.
Nb addition will raise uniform tensile elongation by at least 20–30%, from about 13.5% to about 17% or higher.
The Nb-modified alloy will retain yield strength within 5–10% of 786 MPa.
The Nb-modified alloy will retain compressive strength within 5–10% of 1314 MPa.
The Nb-modified alloy's impact-triggered energy release will remain unchanged or improve.
The hypothesis is intended to apply at room temperature and modestly elevated temperatures.
Evaluation will use quasi-static tension at approximately 10^-3 s^-1, matched compression, and impact testing at at least 10^3 s^-1.
The baseline and Nb-modified ingots will be processed identically and directly compared.
The hypothesis is falsified by less than 10% elongation improvement or by a greater than 5–10% deviation in yield strength, compressive strength, or impact energy release.
Nb may instead cause adverse phase transformations or degradation of other mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The success target is at least a 20–30% elongation increase, but failure is defined as less than 10% improvement. Outcomes between 10% and the stated 20–30% target are neither successful nor falsifying.
Impact energy release is allowed to improve, yet the falsification rule rejects a deviation greater than ±5–10%; this would classify an improvement greater than 5–10% as falsifying.
The 13.5% value is identified as terminal tensile strain but is then used as the baseline for uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct measurements.
